title: Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) differentially impact the in vitro inflammatory response of murine microglial cells.

sections.abstract: <jats:p> Long‐chain omega‐3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (n‐3 PUFA) have anti‐inflammatory activity <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>in vivo</jats:italic> . Microglia are macrophage‐like immune cells of the central nervous system (CNS) that produce pro‐inflammatory molecules which exacerbates many CNS diseases. In this study, we evaluated the <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic> bioactivity of two n‐3 PUFA: DHA and EPA. BV‐2 cells, a murine microglial cell line, as well as primary microglial cells were used in these studies. Fatty acid analysis of BV‐2 cells indicated that this cell line was deficient in long‐chain PUFA compared with freshly isolated primary microglia. To correct this deficiency, BV‐2 cells were co‐incubated with arachidonic acid and DHA (@40 & 20 μM, respectfully) for 24 h. PUFA were complexed to albumin prior to use. This pre‐treatment successfully “normalized” membrane PUFA content to that found in primary microglia. The production of interleukin (IL)‐6 and IL‐1β, but not tumor necrosis factor (TNF)‐α and nitric oxide (NO), was decreased by the normalization of BV‐2 fatty acid profile (p< 0.05). Furthermore, production of NO, IL‐6, IL‐1β, and TNF‐α were significantly diminished by the additional treatment of BV‐2 cells with 50 μM DHA, but not EPA (p< 0.05). Similarly, DHA treatment of primary microglia diminished production of IL‐6 and TNF‐α, while EPA had no effect. In conclusion, these data demonstrate that two closely related n‐3 PUFA differentially impact pro‐inflammatory responses of murine microglia. We believe these data suggest that dietary DHA may be more beneficial than EPA at modulating inflammatory diseases of the CNS. </jats:p>
